Female Western toads attain a maximum snout-vent length of 13 centimeters [Li = 13 centimeters], a size that considerably exceeds that of males, which reach an ultimate SVL of 11.5 centimeters [Li = 11.5 centimeters]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is common among bufonids and is thought to reflect differential energetic investments in gamete production versus mate acquisition. The largest females correspondingly achieve an ultimate wet body mass of 92.9 grams [Wwi = 92.9 grams], while males plateau at a substantially lower adult body mass of 64.6 grams [Wwi = 64.6 grams]. These asymptotic masses are consistent with the robust, terrestrial body plan typical of the genus Anaxyrus and represent the upper bounds of somatic growth under favorable conditions in montane and lowland habitats alike.

Newly deposited eggs of the Western toad are encased within a protective gelatinous matrix, and each individual embryonated egg has a computed wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams], based on the typical spherical diameter of 1 to 2 millimeters. Incubation at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C] yields a brief embryonic period, with eclosion occurring after just 6 days [ab = 6 days]. Upon hatching, the resulting yolk-sac larva remains endotrophic for a short interval before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The timing of this hatching event is critically sensitive to thermal conditions; at cooler temperatures typical of high-elevation breeding ponds, development proceeds more slowly, but under the controlled laboratory conditions described here, the age at birth is reliably recorded at 28 °C.

Following the onset of exogenous feeding, tadpoles embark on a period of rapid somatic growth that culminates in the larval-juvenile transition. At a constant water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the time from hatching to metamorphosis is precisely 43 days , during which the free-swimming larva progresses through successive Gosner stages, developing hind limb buds and undergoing tail resorption. At metamorphic climax, the recently transformed toadlet exhibits a snout-vent length of 1.4 centimeters  and a corresponding wet weight at metamorphosis of 0.115 grams . This relatively small size at the terrestrial transition reflects the limited nutrient storage capacity of the herbivorous tadpole stage and imposes a period of elevated vulnerability to desiccation and predation in the terrestrial environment.

The post-metamorphic juvenile phase is characterized by sustained feeding and growth before the onset of gonadal maturation. Under field conditions, the time from metamorphosis to puberty has been estimated at approximately 1095 days following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 1095 days following metamorphosis] when ambient temperatures average around 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This extended juvenile period reflects the slow maturation typical of high-elevation amphibians, where short growing seasons and limited prey availability constrain energy acquisition. In populations inhabiting warmer lowland sites, maturation may be accelerated, but published accounts consistently report that puberty is delayed until the third year following metamorphosis in most of the species' range.

Reproductive output in this species is substantial, with gravid females depositing a single clutch of approximately 5200 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 5200 eggs per spawning event] annually, a rate of one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year] that is typical of large-bodied bufonids. This annual egg production is achieved under average spring breeding temperatures of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], which synchronize with optimal pond conditions for larval development. Maximum recorded longevity for Western toads under natural conditions has been documented at about 11.5 years [am = about 11.5 years] for individuals experiencing average annual temperatures near 20 °C, indicating a relatively slow life-history pace for an anuran of this body size at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C].
